question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

1.text:
After OLL the U face is monochromatic.  The only information that is left
in the last layer is the permutation of the 8 U-layer pieces and that
information lives on the side of the U-layer.

The U-layer has

* 4 U-edges : 1 U-sticker + 1 side-sticker
* 4 U-corners : 1 U-sticker + 2 side-stickers

so that the U-layer contributes 9 U-stickers and 4+8 = 12 side stickers
to the cube.  Up to rotation the 12 side stickers of the top slice are

 Front top row 3, Right top row 3, Back top row 3, Left top row 3

and they are the only stickers that can distinguish one PLL permutation
from another.  In the strict sense you have to be able to read the 12
non-U stickers of the U-slice, 4 edge side stickers and 8 corner side
stickers, i.e. the 12 stickers that belong to the U-slice but are not on
U itself.

In practice the permutation is over-determined.  The information
theoretic content of the 21 PLL classes is log2 21≈4.4 bit, i.e. three
well chosen side stickers already carry enough information and a normal
human recognition is done with the 6 stickers that are visible on the
three faces you are looking at, 3 front + 3 right, or, what is the same
thing, with the 4 edge side stickers and the 4 one-per-corner side
stickers, 8 distinct side stickers, 12 physical side stickers in total,
and the last piece is then forced by parity.  This is the usual
“look at the four edges and the four corners of the U-slice’’ description
of PLL recognition. ∎

4.text:
In CFOP the U face is already colour solved after OLL so the U stickers
themselves carry no information. What is left is the permutation of the
8 U layer pieces

* 4 U edges : UF, UR, UB, UL
* 4 U corners : UFR, UBR, UBL, UFL

on the U ring. A U edge is completely identified by the one side sticker
that it shows on the face it sits on and a U corner is completely
identified up to the OLL orientation by one of its two side stickers.
Hence one side identifying sticker per U layer piece is enough and
eight distinct non-U identifying stickers, four edge and four corner,
are in principle sufficient to read the permutation.

In practice you read the whole U ring. The U ring is made of

* 4 edges × 1 side sticker = 4 side stickers
* 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 8 side stickers

12 non-U stickers in all, the 8 of them which are the identifying
stickers being the 4 edge side stickers and one side sticker per corner.
That is the information that is normally spoken of as “the side
colours of the last layer”.  The 8 identifying stickers are the minimal
information; the whole U ring is 12 non-U stickers.

2.text:
In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face monochrome.  Up to a rotation of the
cube the U face is therefore the same for every PLL and it carries no
information at all.  What is left to be decided is the permutation of the
eight U-layer pieces

* 4 U edges – each of them is completely identified by the one side
sticker that is not on U,
* 4 U corners – each of them is completely identified by the (unordered)
pair of side stickers that is not on U.

Modulo a whole-cube rotation the permutation of the four U edges is
$4!/4=6$ essentially different and the permutation of the four U corners is
$4!/4=6$ essentially different.  The $6\times 6=36$ possibilities are
reduced by the parity condition to the 21 essentially different PLL
permutations.

Hence in principle you have to know which physical piece is sitting in each
of the eight U positions.  One side sticker is enough to name an U edge and
one side sticker is enough to name a U corner up to the mirror that is
resolved by the other pieces, i.e. one non-U sticker per U piece.  That is

* 4 edge side stickers,
* 4 corner side stickers,

8 distinct non-U stickers in total, the 12 physical side stickers of the
U-layer

4 edges ×1 + 4 corners ×2 =12 stickers being the whole U-layer side
information.  In particular the four edge side stickers together with any
four corner side stickers, e.g. the eight stickers that are visible on the
front and right faces of the U layer, are enough to name the eight U pieces
and therefore to name the 21 PLL permutations.  This is the 12-sticker
U-layer side information that is normally spoken of as the “8 pieces’’ of
PLL information, four edges + four corners.  Up to the usual rotation
ambiguity this can be reduced in practice to seven independent non-U
stickers, four edges + three corners, which is the information theoretic
$ \log_{4}21\approx 2.2$ stickers $\approx 4\!-\!8$ sticker lower bound that
is normally quoted as the eight-piece, i.e. the twelve physical side-sticker,
recognition of PLL. ∎

3.text:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented when you get to PLL so the nine
U stickers are all the same colour and carry no permutation information
at all.  What you are recognising is the permutation of the four U edges
and the four U corners, and the permutation is carried in the side
colours of the U layer.

The U layer contains

* 4 U edges : 1 side sticker per piece = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U corners : 2 side stickers per piece = 8 non-U stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers in total.  That is the information that is
available to you.  In practice you never have to read the whole 12
sticker set.  Information theoretically

log4 21 < 3

so three side stickers are enough in principle to distinguish the 21
essentially different PLL classes, and in ordinary recognition you are
looking at the side colour of the four U edges and the side colour of a
couple of the U corners.  The usual working figure quoted is the four
edge side stickers together with two corner side stickers, i.e. six to
eight non-U stickers, which is the side-colour information of the U
layer.  The nine U stickers themselves are completely uninformative
for PLL, the whole of the PLL information lives on the 12 side stickers
of the U layer. ∎

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is PLL recognition after OLL in CFOP. All colleagues agree the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. The information lives in the side stickers of the U-slice.

U-slice side inventory:
* 4 U edges: 1 side sticker each = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U corners: 2 side stickers each = 8 non-U stickers
Total physical non-U stickers in the top slice = 12. The 9 U stickers are uninformative for PLL.

Consensus points:
* The whole U-layer side information is 12 stickers.
* A U edge is identified by its single side sticker; a U corner is identified up to orientation by its two side stickers, so one identifying sticker per piece is enough.
* Hence minimally 8 distinct identifying stickers, 4 edge side + 4 corner side, are sufficient to name the 8 U pieces and therefore the 21 PLL classes. Those 8 distinct stickers correspond to the 12 physical side stickers.

Divergence / nuance:
* Colleague 1: strict reading = 12 non-U stickers of the U-slice; in practice over-determined, recognition is done with the 6-8 stickers visible on front+right etc.
* Colleague 2: 8 distinct non-U stickers suffice, 12 physical; up to whole-cube rotation and parity the independent count can be reduced to ~7 independent non-U stickers.
* Colleague 3: 12 total available; information-theoretically log4 21 <3 so three well-chosen stickers suffice in principle; usual working figure quoted as 6-8 non-U stickers.
* Colleague 4: one side identifier per piece → 8 identifying stickers minimal; whole U ring is 12 non-U stickers.

Unresolved for me: whether the question asks for the strict physical count of side stickers that exist on the U-layer, i.e. 12, or the minimal distinct identifying set, i.e. 8 distinct / 12 physical, or the information-theoretic independent minimum ~7. The most literal strict answer is 12 non-top-facing stickers of the U-slice; the practical minimal identifying set is 8 distinct stickers. Keep both interpretations for later rounds.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is about PLL recognition after OLL in CFOP, i.e. U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information.

All colleagues agree the PLL information lives only on the U-layer side stickers, not on the 9 U stickers.
* U-layer side content: 4 U-edges each contribute 1 side sticker = 4 stickers; 4 U-corners each contribute 2 side stickers = 8 stickers. 12 physical non-U stickers in total on the U-ring.

The disagreement is about how many of those need to be *seen* / are *independent* for identification.

* Strict physical set: 12 non-U stickers of the U-slice, 4 edge side + 8 corner side, are the only stickers that can distinguish one PLL from another. Up to whole-cube rotation the 12 stickers are the Front/ Right/ Back/ Left top rows.
* Identifying set: one side sticker is enough to name a U-edge, and one side sticker is enough to name a U-corner up to the mirror resolved by the other pieces. That gives 4 edge side + 4 corner side = 8 distinct identifying stickers. The 12 physical stickers contain redundancy, 2 per corner.
* Practical reduction: because the 21 essentially different PLL classes have log2 21≈4.4 bits, three well-chosen side stickers are information-theoretically enough, and with parity the eight pieces are over-determined. Commonly quoted working minima are 6–8 stickers, e.g. the four edge side stickers plus 3–4 corner side stickers, with Colleague 2 noting 7 independent non-U stickers up to rotation/parity, and Colleague 1 noting the usual human recognition uses the 6 stickers visible on two faces, i.e. 8 distinct side stickers in total.

Unresolved nuance for the question: does “must be seen” mean the total physical information content of the U-ring =12 non-U stickers, the minimal distinct identifying set =8 stickers, or the information-theoretic/parity reduced minimum ≈7, ≈3-4 stickers. Current belief is the canonical teaching statement is the 12 side stickers of the U-layer, with the minimal sufficient distinct set being 8 stickers, 4 edge +4 corner, reducible to ~7 independent.
